title: Business Intelligence Basics: Designing Systems that Drive Decisions
subtitle: Design a business intelligence system that turns scattered data into regular, trusted decisions for leaders and teams.
description: This course teaches BI as a system, not a tool. You will map decisions, assess data sources, write metric definitions, design a reporting structure and a governance plan, and learn to scope, price and lead BI work in African organisations.
outcomes: Build a decision inventory and score an organisation's BI maturity
Create a data source map and a metric dictionary with owners and exclusions
Prioritise decisions and design strategic, tactical and operational reporting tiers
Write a governance plan covering data quality, metric ownership and data protection
Run discovery, price a BI strategy engagement and control its scope
Plan adoption, measure impact and present a BI strategy case study
audience: Women with some spreadsheet or reporting experience who want to lead how an organisation uses data, as an employee, manager or consultant.
tools: Google Sheets or Excel for the design documents
Access to an organisation you can study (your own business, employer, cooperative or NGO)

modules.title: What BI Is and Where It Fits
modules.overview: You learn what a business intelligence system is, the vocabulary professionals use, and how to judge how mature an organisation's BI already is. By the end you can describe any organisation's starting point and its next sensible step.

lessons.title: From data to decisions: what a BI system really is
objectives: Explain business intelligence as a system that serves decisions, not as a single tool
Name the six links in the BI chain from source systems to action
Build the first lines of a decision inventory for a real business
Spot the common signs of a business that has data but no BI system

blocks.text: Many businesses already have plenty of data. The POS terminal records every card payment, Paystack or Moniepoint keeps every transfer, the shop has a stock book, and the manager has a spreadsheet. Yet the owner still asks on Monday morning: "How much did we really sell last week, and what should I reorder?" and nobody can answer quickly with confidence. That gap is what **business intelligence (BI)** closes.

In this course, BI means **a deliberate, repeating system that gets the right information to the right decision-maker at the right time, so that a decision is made and acted on**. A dashboard is one part of it. Excel, SQL or Power BI are tools inside it. The system is the whole chain, plus the people and routines that keep it alive.

blocks.name: business-decisions
blocks.alt: A person choosing between options on a board
blocks.caption: BI starts with the decisions people must make, then works back to the data.

blocks.text: The six links in the BI chain

blocks.title: The BI chain
items: Source systems
Collect and clean
One trusted store
Defined metrics
Reports and alerts
Decision and action
blocks.caption: Information is only useful when every link works, from where data is born to what someone does with it.

items: **Source systems**: where data is born. POS, payment apps, accounting software, school or clinic software, WhatsApp order lists, paper registers.
**Collect and clean**: getting data out (exports, connectors, typing) and fixing spellings, duplicates and missing values. Professionals call this ETL: extract, transform, load.
**One trusted store**: a single place where the cleaned data lives. For a small business this can be one well-structured Google Sheet; for a bank it is a data warehouse.
**Defined metrics**: written definitions so that "sales" or "active customer" means the same thing in every report.
**Reports and alerts**: the delivery: a weekly one-page summary, a dashboard, a WhatsApp message when stock is low.
**Decision and action**: a named person looks at the information on a known day and decides something. Without this last link, the rest is decoration.

blocks.text: If any link breaks, the whole chain fails. A beautiful dashboard built on an export that nobody refreshes shows last month's numbers. A correct number delivered to the wrong person, or on the wrong day, changes nothing.
Start with decisions, not data

Beginners usually start by asking "What data do we have?" and then build charts of everything. BI designers start with a different question: **"What decisions does this business make again and again, and what would make them better?"** The tool for this is a **decision inventory**: a simple table listing each recurring decision, who makes it, how often, what information they need, where that information comes from today, and what is missing.

blocks.title: Worked example: a decision inventory for a frozen-food distributor
blocks.context: Funmi (for example) runs a frozen chicken and fish distribution business in Ibadan with two cold rooms. Each cold room manager counts stock by hand every Friday, which takes about 3 hours.
steps: She lists five decisions she makes repeatedly: weekly reorder from suppliers, credit limits for retail customers, delivery van routes, monthly price review, and whether to open a third cold room.
For each decision she writes the owner and frequency. Reorder: Funmi, weekly. Credit limits: Funmi and her accountant, monthly. Routes: the logistics supervisor, daily.

She writes the information each one needs. Reorder needs stock on hand by product, sales in the last four weeks, and supplier lead time. Credit limits need each customer's purchases and how many days they take to pay.

She notes the current source and the gap. Stock comes from the Friday hand count (slow, no history kept). Customer payment days are not tracked at all: transfers sit in the bank app with no link to invoices.
She works out the cost of the manual count: 2 cold rooms x 3 hours x 52 weeks = 312 staff hours a year, and the result is thrown away after each reorder.
blocks.result: Funmi now sees that her two most valuable gaps are stock history and customer payment days. Her BI work should start there, not with a sales chart she already understands.

head: Decision
Owner
How often
Information needed
Today's source
Gap
rows: Stock by product, 4-week sales, lead time
Purchases and days to pay per customer

blocks.text: Signs that a business has data but no BI system

items: Two reports show different totals for the same month, and nobody knows which is right.
Monthly reports take days to compile, and arrive after the decision was already made.
Reports are sent but nobody can name a decision that changed because of them.
Each manager keeps a private spreadsheet, and the numbers live only in their phone.
Questions like "which customers pay late?" need someone to dig through months of records by hand.

blocks.title: A tool is not a system
blocks.text: Buying Power BI or hiring someone who knows SQL does not create BI. Without agreed decisions, clean sources, written definitions and a routine for using the reports, the new tool simply produces faster confusion.

This course is about designing the whole system. Other WODDI Institute courses teach specific tools in depth, such as Excel dashboards, SQL and Power BI. Here you learn to decide what should be built, in what order, for whom, and how to keep it trustworthy. That is the work of a BI lead or BI consultant.

takeaways: BI is a repeating system that delivers the right information to the right person at the right time
The chain runs from source systems to a decision and an action; every link must work
Start with a decision inventory, not with the data you happen to have
Different totals, late reports and unread reports are signs of BI missing

activity.title: Draft your first decision inventory
steps: Choose a business you know well: your own, an employer, a church or cooperative
List five decisions it makes at least once a month
For each, write the owner, how often, and the information needed
Write where that information comes from today and the main gap
Circle the two decisions where better information would save the most money or time
activity.evidence: A photo or file of your five-row decision inventory with two decisions circled

lessons.title: The language of BI: analytics types, OLTP and OLAP, ETL, warehouses and grain
objectives: Classify a business question as descriptive, diagnostic, predictive or prescriptive
Explain the difference between a system that runs the business and a store built for analysis
Describe ETL, ELT, data warehouse, data mart and data lake in plain words
Declare the grain of a table and calculate how many rows it will hold

blocks.text: When you work with IT staff, software vendors or data engineers, they will use words that sound difficult. Each one names a simple idea. Learning them lets you lead the conversation, ask the right questions and check what you are being sold.

blocks.name: database-tables
blocks.alt: Linked database tables on a screen
blocks.caption: Most BI vocabulary describes how data moves from the systems that record it into tables built for answering questions.

blocks.text: Four kinds of question

head: Type
Question it answers
Example for a provisions wholesaler
rows: Sales fell because two big retail customers stopped buying
At the current pace, rice stock will run out in 9 days
Reorder 120 bags of rice today to cover the lead time

blocks.text: Most real BI value in small and mid-sized organisations comes from doing descriptive and diagnostic work well and regularly. Predictive work needs clean history first. Be cautious of anyone who promises "AI predictions" for a business whose sales records are still in three notebooks.
Systems that run the business versus systems that answer questions

blocks.title: OLTP versus OLAP
items: OLTP: runs the business
OLAP: answers questions
left: Records one sale at a time
Must be fast and always on
blocks.caption: Running heavy reports directly on the till system slows it down and loses history, so BI copies data into a separate store.

blocks.text: **OLTP** (online transaction processing) systems record day-to-day transactions: a sale, a payment, an enrolment. **OLAP** (online analytical processing) means storage and tools designed for analysis: adding up thousands of rows, comparing months, slicing by branch. BI almost always copies data out of OLTP systems into an analytical store, so reports do not slow down the till and history is kept even when the source system overwrites old values.
Moving data: ETL and ELT

items: **ETL**: extract data from the source, transform it (clean, rename, join, calculate), then load the clean result into the store.
**ELT**: extract and load the raw data first, then transform it inside the store. Common with cloud warehouses that have plenty of computing power.
Either way, the transform rules must be written down, because they decide what every number means.

blocks.text: Where data is kept

items: **Data warehouse**: a central, structured store of cleaned, integrated data from many sources, kept over time for reporting.
**Data mart**: a smaller slice of the warehouse for one department, for example finance or sales.
**Data lake**: a large store of raw files of many kinds (exports, logs, images), often kept before anyone has decided how to use them. Without discipline it becomes a "data swamp".

blocks.text: Ask any vendor which of these they are actually offering. A product described as a "data platform" might be a warehouse, a lake, a dashboard tool or all three, and the answer changes the cost, the skills needed and who will maintain it.
For a small business, the "warehouse" may honestly be one Google Sheet with a clean sales table and a clean customer table. The idea is the same: one trusted place, separate from the source apps.
Grain, facts and dimensions

The Kimball Group, whose dimensional modelling methods are widely used in BI, puts it simply: the grain "establishes exactly what a single fact table row represents". It must be declared before you choose anything else, and different grains should never be mixed in one table. **Facts** are the numbers you add up (quantity, amount). **Dimensions** are the things you slice by (date, branch, product, customer).

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing the grain for a supermarket's sales table
blocks.context: Ngozi (for example) is designing a sales table for a supermarket with 3 branches, about 400 products, and around 250 receipts per branch per day, each with about 4 items.
steps: Option A grain: one row per product per branch per day. Maximum rows in a 30-day month: 3 x 400 x 30 = 36,000 rows (fewer in practice, because not every product sells every day).
Option B grain: one row per receipt line (one item on one receipt). Rows per day: 3 branches x 250 receipts x 4 lines = 3,000. Per 30-day month: 3,000 x 30 = 90,000 rows.
She checks the questions in the decision inventory. The owner wants to know which payment method customers use at different hours, and which products are bought together.
Option A cannot answer either question, because it has no receipt, no time and no payment method. Option B can.
She chooses Option B, the most detailed (atomic) grain, and writes the declaration at the top of the table: "One row = one item line on one receipt."
blocks.result: The table holds about 90,000 rows a month, easily handled by Power BI or a database, and it can answer the owner's real questions. Daily totals can always be added up from it, but receipt detail can never be recovered from daily totals.

blocks.title: Two more words you will hear
blocks.text: **Latency** or **refresh frequency** means how old the data is when someone sees it: real-time, hourly, daily or monthly. **Single source of truth** means one agreed store and one agreed definition for each key number. Ask about both in every BI conversation.

takeaways: Most value comes from doing descriptive and diagnostic analysis reliably
Run reports on a separate analytical store, not on the system that records transactions
ETL and ELT both move and clean data; the written transform rules define your numbers
Declare the grain first: one row equals exactly one thing
Detail can be summed up later, but summaries can never be broken back down

activity.title: Translate a business into BI language
steps: Pick one source system in a business you know (POS, payment app, register)
Write one descriptive, one diagnostic, one predictive and one prescriptive question for it
Declare the grain of its main table in one sentence
Estimate rows per month with a simple multiplication
Write whether you would copy the data daily, weekly or monthly, and why
activity.evidence: A note with four questions, a grain statement and your row calculation

lessons.title: BI maturity: assessing where an organisation stands and where the work is
objectives: Describe five levels of BI maturity using concrete signs
Score an organisation with a 10-question maturity check
Choose the right next step for an organisation at each level
Identify the kinds of organisations and roles that need BI design skills

blocks.text: Before you recommend anything, you need to know where an organisation is starting from. A cooperative that keeps contributions in a notebook needs very different help from a bank with ten systems and a data team. A **maturity model** is a simple way to describe that starting point and agree on the next realistic step.

blocks.name: progress-overview
blocks.alt: A person reviewing progress bars on a board
blocks.caption: A maturity check tells you which step comes next, so you do not skip the foundations.

blocks.text: Five levels of BI maturity
Many maturity models exist. This course uses a simple five-level version that you can explain to any manager in five minutes.

blocks.title: BI maturity levels (top is most mature)
items: 5. Decision-driven
4. Managed
3. Centralised
2. Spreadsheet reporting
1. Scattered
blocks.caption: Each level rests on the one below; dashboards at level 4 fail if level 3 foundations are missing.

head: Level
What you see
Best next step
rows: Data in notebooks, phones and people's heads. Reports only when someone asks.
Choose one key process and record it in one shared, structured sheet.
Monthly reports built by hand from exports. Numbers often disagree.
Write metric definitions and create one trusted store for the main data.
One trusted store exists. Standard reports refresh on schedule.
Assign owners to metrics and add data quality checks.
Metric dictionary, owners, access rules, quality checks, change log.
Link each report to a decision meeting and track actions taken.
Reports are used in fixed review meetings; alerts trigger action; results are tracked.
Add forecasting and deeper analysis where history is reliable.

blocks.text: A 10-question maturity check

Score each question 0 (no), 1 (partly) or 2 (yes). The maximum is 20. Use the total as a guide, then confirm with what you see: 0 to 5 suggests level 1, 6 to 9 level 2, 10 to 13 level 3, 14 to 17 level 4, and 18 to 20 level 5.

items: Are the main transactions (sales, payments, enrolments, donations) recorded digitally?
Is there one agreed place where cleaned data for reporting is kept?
Are key metrics written down with a formula and an owner?
Do standard reports refresh on a schedule without someone rebuilding them?
Does the same number appear the same in every report?
Can managers get the information they need within a day of asking?
Are there routine checks for missing, duplicate or invalid records?
Is access to personal and financial data limited to the right people?
Are reports reviewed in a regular meeting where decisions are recorded?
Can the organisation name a decision that changed because of a report in the last three months?

blocks.title: Worked example: scoring a thrift and credit cooperative
blocks.context: Hauwa (for example) is the new administrator of a cooperative in Kaduna with about 600 members. Contributions are paid by bank transfer and recorded in Excel by two officers.
steps: She scores the ten questions: 2 (contributions are digital), 1 (two separate Excel files), 0 (no written definitions), 0 (reports rebuilt each month), 0 (the two files often disagree), 1 (answers take about a week), 0 (no checks), 1 (files are shared on WhatsApp but only among officers), 1 (monthly executive meeting, no decision log), 0 (nobody can name a changed decision).
A score of 6 falls in the 6 to 9 band: level 2, spreadsheet reporting.
From the table, the next step is to agree definitions (for example, what makes a member "in good standing") and merge the two files into one trusted register.
blocks.result: The cooperative is at level 2. Hauwa recommends one shared register and five written definitions before anyone talks about dashboards.

blocks.title: Do not skip levels
blocks.text: A common and costly mistake is buying a dashboard tool for a level 1 or level 2 organisation. The dashboard looks impressive at the launch, then shows wrong or stale numbers, and leaders stop trusting data altogether. Fix the foundations first.
Where BI design work is found
Any organisation with several systems, several managers and recurring decisions needs BI thinking. In Nigeria and across Africa this includes:

items: **Distribution and retail**: FMCG distributors, pharmacies and supermarkets with several branches, POS terminals and stock to manage.
**Financial services**: banks, microfinance banks, cooperatives and fintechs tracking loans, repayments and customer activity.
**Education**: private schools and training centres tracking fees, enrolment, attendance and results.
**Health**: clinics, hospitals and diagnostic labs tracking patients, services, stock and claims.
**NGOs and programmes**: organisations that must report to donors on reach and results across several states or countries.
**Government agencies and associations**: registrations, revenue and service delivery records.

blocks.text: Roles you will see advertised include **BI analyst** (builds reports and answers questions), **BI developer** (builds data models and dashboards), **data engineer** (builds pipelines and warehouses), **analytics engineer** (turns raw data into clean, documented tables) and **BI lead or manager** (owns the strategy, priorities and governance). This course prepares you for the strategy and design side, which is often missing even when tool skills are present.

Local realities shape good design: expensive mobile data, unreliable power, many people working only on phones, and a lot of business happening on WhatsApp. A good BI design for a Nigerian SME may deliver a short PDF or image summary on WhatsApp each Monday rather than expect managers to open a heavy dashboard.

takeaways: Maturity describes the starting point and the next realistic step
Score with the 10-question check, then confirm with what you observe
Fix definitions and one trusted store before building dashboards
BI design skills are needed wherever several systems feed recurring decisions
Design for local realities: phones, data costs, power and WhatsApp

activity.title: Run a maturity check
steps: Choose an organisation you know or work with
Score all ten questions honestly with 0, 1 or 2
Add the scores and find the level
Write one sentence of evidence for your two lowest scores
Write the single next step you would recommend
activity.evidence: A completed 10-question score sheet with total, level and recommended next step

quiz.q: A pharmacy owner has a new Power BI dashboard, but the stock numbers come from an export that nobody refreshes after the first week. Which link in the BI chain is broken?
options: Defined metrics
Collect and clean (getting data out regularly)
Decision and action
Reports and alerts
quiz.explain: The delivery exists, but data is not being collected and loaded on a schedule, so the dashboard shows stale numbers.

quiz.q: What should a BI designer create first for a new client?
options: A dashboard with every available chart
A data lake for all the client's files
A decision inventory of recurring decisions and the information they need
A predictive model of next year's sales
quiz.explain: BI starts with decisions. The inventory shows which information matters and where the gaps are.

quiz.q: A table has the grain "one row per product per branch per day". The business has 2 branches and 250 products. What is the maximum number of rows in a 30-day month?
"Sales dropped in March because the Lekki branch was closed for 10 days." What kind of analysis is this?
options: Descriptive
Diagnostic
Predictive
Prescriptive
quiz.explain: It explains why something happened, which is diagnostic analysis.

quiz.q: A school scores 7 out of 20 on the maturity check. Fees reports are rebuilt by hand each month and the bursar's and principal's totals often differ. What is the best next step?
options: Buy a dashboard tool and train all staff
Write metric definitions and create one trusted store for fees data
Start predicting next term's enrolment
Hire a data engineer to build a data lake
quiz.explain: A score of 7 is level 2. The next step is shared definitions and one trusted store, not advanced tools.

quiz.q: Why does BI usually copy data out of the POS or payments system into a separate store?
options: Because POS systems cannot store numbers
So heavy reports do not slow the transaction system and history is kept
Because the law requires two copies of all data
So that staff cannot see sales
quiz.explain: Transaction (OLTP) systems are built to record one transaction quickly; analysis needs a separate store that keeps history.

modules.title: Designing the BI System: Tools, Workflow and Trust
modules.overview: You turn decisions into a blueprint: a data source map, a metric dictionary, a prioritised reporting structure and a governance plan. These are the documents that make any BI tool produce numbers people trust and use.

lessons.title: The BI design toolkit: data source map, metric dictionary and technology stack
objectives: Build a data source map that rates each system on access, quality and refresh
Write a complete metric dictionary entry with formula, owner and exclusions
Choose a sensible technology stack for a small, medium or large organisation
Explain how the decision inventory, source map and metric dictionary connect

blocks.text: BI design depends more on a few well-kept documents than on any single software product. You already know the first one, the **decision inventory**. This lesson adds two more: the **data source map** and the **metric dictionary**. Together they become the blueprint that any tool, from Google Sheets to Power BI, can then implement.

blocks.name: organizing-data
blocks.alt: A person arranging data cards into order
blocks.caption: The source map and metric dictionary organise what exists before anything is built.

blocks.title: How the design documents connect
items: Decision inventory
Data source map
Metric dictionary
Reporting design
Build in chosen tool
blocks.caption: Each document answers a question the next one depends on: which decisions, which data, which definitions, which reports.

blocks.text: The data source map

A data source map lists every system that holds data needed by the decision inventory. For each system you record: what it records, who owns it, how data can be taken out (manual export, scheduled export, connector or API, or retyping), how often it changes, known quality problems, and whether it contains **personal data** such as names, phone numbers or health details.

To compare sources quickly, rate three things from 1 (poor) to 3 (good): **access** (how easy it is to get the data out), **quality** (how complete and correct it is) and **frequency** (how fresh it can be). The total, out of 9, shows which sources are ready to use now and which need work first.

blocks.title: Worked example: mapping a private school's data sources
blocks.context: Blessing (for example) is designing BI for a private secondary school in Abuja. The proprietor's top decisions are fee follow-up, staffing per class and which students need academic support.
steps: She finds four sources: fee payments (bank statements and the Paystack dashboard export), the student register (an Excel file kept by the admin officer), results (a school management app that exports CSV) and attendance (paper registers in each class).
Fee payments: access 3 (CSV export), quality 2 (some parents pay with a sibling's name as reference), frequency 3 (daily). Total 8.
Student register: access 3, quality 2 (duplicate names after transfers), frequency 2 (updated each term). Total 7.
Results app: access 2 (export only by the vice principal), quality 3, frequency 1 (once a term). Total 6.
Attendance registers: access 1 (paper), quality 2, frequency 1 (would need weekly typing). Total 4.
blocks.result: Fees and the student register (8 and 7) are ready for a first report. Attendance (4) needs a simple digital register before it can feed any decision, so Blessing puts it in phase two.

blocks.text: The metric dictionary

A **metric dictionary** is the single written definition of every key number. Without it, the bursar, the principal and the proprietor will each calculate "fees collected" slightly differently, and the first meeting with the new report becomes an argument. Each entry has:

items: **Name** and plain-language meaning
**Formula**, with exactly which records are included and excluded
**Source** and the field names used
**Owner**: the one person who approves any change to the definition
**Refresh**: how often it updates, and when
**Target or threshold**, if any, and who set it

head: Field
Entry: Fee collection rate
rows: Share of this term's billed fees that has been received
Fees received for the term divided by fees billed for the term, x 100
Tuition and compulsory levies billed this term
Students on full scholarship; optional items such as excursions
Billing sheet (billed), bank and Paystack exports matched to student ID (received)

blocks.text: Notice the exclusions. If scholarship students are left in the billed figure, the rate looks worse than it really is, and the proprietor may chase the wrong families. A definition is only complete when it says what is left out.
Choosing a technology stack
Choose tools to fit the organisation's size, skills, budget and devices, not to impress. A stack that the staff can keep running after you leave is better than a powerful one they cannot maintain.

head: Size
Trusted store
Collect and clean
Delivery
rows: One structured Google Sheet or Excel workbook
Manual exports pasted into a raw tab, cleaned with formulas
Google's free Data Studio (formerly Looker Studio) or a one-page summary sent on WhatsApp
Excel or a small database such as PostgreSQL
Power BI (Desktop for building, the Power BI service for sharing) or Data Studio
A data warehouse, on-premises or in the cloud
Automated pipelines run by data engineers
Enterprise BI platform with access controls

blocks.title: Check the devices
blocks.text: Ask how managers will actually view reports. Microsoft describes Power BI Desktop as a Windows app for building reports, so a team that only has phones and Macs will view through the service or mobile app, and someone still needs a Windows machine to build. Design around what people really use.

takeaways: Three documents form the BI blueprint: decision inventory, source map, metric dictionary
Rate each source on access, quality and frequency to decide what is ready now
A metric definition must state its formula, exclusions, owner and refresh
Pick the simplest stack the organisation can keep running

activity.title: Map sources and define two metrics
steps: Take the decision inventory you drafted in Module 1
List every source system those decisions depend on
Rate each source 1 to 3 on access, quality and frequency and total the scores
Write full metric dictionary entries for the two most important numbers
Suggest a stack (store, cleaning method, delivery) with one reason
activity.evidence: A source map table with scores and two completed metric dictionary entries

lessons.title: From discovery to rollout: prioritising decisions and designing the reporting structure
objectives: Score decisions on value and feasibility and place them on a priority matrix
Design strategic, tactical and operational report tiers with the right cadence
Plan a small first release and a launch routine that gets reports used
Write a one-page reporting structure for an organisation

blocks.text: A decision inventory for even a small organisation can list 20 or more decisions. You cannot serve them all at once. Professional BI work moves in a clear sequence: **discover, prioritise, design the reporting structure, build the smallest useful version, launch it into a real meeting, then measure use and improve**. This lesson covers the middle steps: prioritising and designing.

blocks.name: scrum-board
blocks.alt: A person moving task cards across a board
blocks.caption: Prioritising decisions turns a long wish list into a short, ordered build plan.

blocks.text: Step 1: score value and feasibility

For each decision, score two things from 1 to 5. **Value**: how much money, time or risk depends on getting it right. **Feasibility**: how ready the data is (use your source map scores) and how easy the report is to build. Multiply the two for a priority score out of 25.

blocks.title: Decision priority matrix
items: Major projects: plan carefully
Quick wins: do first
Avoid for now
Fill-ins: do when convenient
blocks.caption: High-value, high-feasibility decisions come first; high-value but low-feasibility ones need data work before reports.

blocks.title: Worked example: prioritising a beverage distributor's decisions
blocks.context: Chidi (for example) leads BI for a soft drinks distributor in Onitsha with three depots and twelve sales reps. Discovery produced six decisions.
steps: Weekly reorder per depot: value 5, feasibility 4, score 5 x 4 = 20.
Monthly sales rep incentives: value 4, feasibility 4, score 16.
Retailer credit limits: value 5, feasibility 3, score 15.
Product price changes: value 4, feasibility 2, score 8.
Delivery route planning: value 3, feasibility 2, score 6.
Opening a fourth depot: value 5, feasibility 1, score 5 (once a year, needs data the company does not yet collect).
blocks.result: Chidi builds for reorder (20), incentives (16) and credit limits (15) first. The fourth depot decision is valuable but not feasible yet, so he adds "start recording retailer locations" to the data work plan instead.

blocks.text: Step 2: design the reporting tiers

Different people need different views at different speeds. A strong reporting structure has three tiers. Each tier answers different questions, so they should not be squeezed into one crowded dashboard.

head: Tier
Audience
Cadence
What it shows
Format
rows: 5 to 8 headline metrics against targets, 12-month trends
One page, with three written insights
Breakdowns by branch, product, rep or programme; what changed and why
Dashboard page or short report per manager
Lists to act on: low stock items, overdue payers, today's deliveries
Alert, exception list or WhatsApp message

blocks.text: Notice that operational reports are mostly **lists of things to act on**, not charts. A supervisor needs "these 7 retailers are more than 30 days overdue, call them today", not a pie chart of overdue balances.
Step 3: the rhythm of business
Each report should be tied to a fixed moment when someone uses it. Write a simple calendar, sometimes called the **rhythm of business**:

items: Daily, 8 am: depot supervisors receive the low-stock and overdue-retailer lists.
Monday, 10 am: weekly sales meeting uses the tactical dashboard, refreshed by 9 am.
First Thursday of the month: management meeting reviews the strategic page and records decisions.
Quarterly: board pack includes the strategic page with quarter-on-quarter trends.

blocks.text: When a report has no meeting or moment attached to it, it will soon stop being read. If nobody can name the meeting, question whether the report should exist.
Sketch each page before building

Before anyone opens a BI tool, sketch each report on paper or in a slide: a **wireframe**. It is far cheaper to move boxes on paper than to rebuild a finished dashboard. Show the sketch to the person who will use the page and ask: "Which decision does this help you make, and is anything missing or unnecessary?"

items: Put the most important number for the decision at the top left, where the eye lands first.
Show every headline number with a comparison: against target, last period or the same period last year. A number alone cannot tell the reader whether to worry.
Print the last refresh date and time on every page, so nobody decides on stale data without knowing it.
Link or footnote each metric to its metric dictionary definition.
Keep a page readable on a phone screen if managers mainly use phones: few numbers, large text, short lists.

blocks.text: Step 4: build small, launch into a real meeting

items: Build the first release for the top two or three decisions only, often in two to four weeks.
Test the numbers with the metric owners before anyone else sees them.
Launch by using the report live in its real meeting, not with a separate presentation.
Write down which decisions were made using it.
Collect feedback after the first three or four uses, then plan the next release.

blocks.title: The everything dashboard
blocks.text: Putting every metric for every audience on one page is the most common design failure. It loads slowly on phones, confuses readers and serves nobody well. Three focused tiers beat one crowded screen.

takeaways: Score each decision on value and feasibility and build the highest first
High-value but low-feasibility decisions need data work before reports
Use three tiers: strategic, tactical, operational, each with its own cadence
Operational reports are action lists, not decorative charts
Tie every report to a fixed meeting or moment in the rhythm of business

activity.title: Design a reporting structure
steps: Score at least five decisions from your inventory on value and feasibility
Multiply and rank them, and choose your top three
Assign each top decision to a tier: strategic, tactical or operational
Write the rhythm of business: who sees what, when, and in which meeting
Describe the first release in three sentences
activity.evidence: A ranked decision table and a one-page reporting structure with cadence

lessons.title: Building trust: data quality checks, metric governance and data protection
objectives: Measure data quality using six recognised dimensions
Set up metric ownership, change control and a certified-report label
Apply data protection practices in line with Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023
Write a short governance plan that keeps a BI system trustworthy over time

blocks.text: A BI system lives or dies on trust. The first time a manager finds a wrong number in a report, they start keeping their own spreadsheet again. **Data quality** keeps the numbers right, **governance** keeps the definitions stable, and **data protection** keeps people's information safe. All three must be designed, not hoped for.

blocks.name: reviewed-docs
blocks.alt: A person checking documents marked as reviewed
blocks.caption: Regular checks and clear ownership are what make people trust the numbers.

blocks.text: Six dimensions of data quality
The UK Government Data Quality Framework, a widely used public reference, names six core dimensions. Each one becomes a simple check you can run every time data is refreshed.

head: Dimension
Meaning
Example check
rows: Share of member records with a phone number
Count of member IDs that appear more than once
Values do not contradict each other
Same customer has the same branch in sales and in the customer list
Data is up to date for the period it represents
Last refresh date shown on every report
Values are in the expected range and format
Dates are real dates; amounts are not negative
Monthly total matches the bank statement

blocks.title: Worked example: scoring a cooperative's member register
blocks.context: Following the maturity check, Hauwa (for example) merges the cooperative's two Excel files into one register of 1,250 member records and checks it before building any report.
steps: Completeness: 75 records have no phone number. Complete records: 1,250 - 75 = 1,175. Score: 1,175 / 1,250 x 100 = 94%.
Uniqueness: 30 records repeat a member ID already in the list. Unique records: 1,250 - 30 = 1,220. Score: 1,220 / 1,250 x 100 = 97.6%.
Validity: 18 records have a joining date in the future or in the wrong format. Valid: 1,232 / 1,250 x 100 = 98.56%, about 98.6%.
Accuracy: total contributions in the register for June are ₦8,460,000; the bank statement shows ₦8,535,000. Difference: ₦75,000, which she traces to three transfers recorded under the wrong month.
She fixes the problems at the source (the officers' entry form now requires a phone number and checks the date) instead of patching the report.
blocks.result: Hauwa removes the 30 duplicates, corrects the three transfers and starts showing the four scores at the bottom of every monthly report, so officers can see quality improve.

blocks.title: The data quality cycle
items: Define the rule
Measure the score
Fix at the source
Monitor each refresh
Review rules quarterly
blocks.caption: Quality is a routine, not a one-time clean-up: problems fixed only in the report will come back next month.

blocks.text: Metric governance
Governance means agreed rules about who decides what. Keep it light but real:

items: **One owner per metric.** Only the owner can approve a change to its definition in the metric dictionary.
**Change log.** Every change records the date, what changed, why, and who approved it, so last year's numbers can still be explained.
**Certified versus exploratory.** Mark reports built from the trusted store and dictionary as certified. Anything else is exploratory and must not be quoted in board papers.
**A data steward.** One person, often part-time, runs the quality checks and keeps the dictionary up to date.
**Quarterly review.** Retire reports nobody uses and review definitions that cause arguments.

blocks.title: One word, three meanings
blocks.text: In many organisations "active member" or "active customer" means something different to each manager: paid this month, paid in the last three months, or simply not closed. Pick one, write it in the dictionary with an owner, and show the definition on the report itself.
Protecting personal data

BI brings personal data from many systems into one place, which raises the risk if something goes wrong. In Nigeria, the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023** set up the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)**, which enforces data protection rules. Read the Act and NDPC guidance for any organisation you advise, and involve the organisation's legal adviser or data protection officer where one exists. Practical design habits:

items: Collect and load only the personal fields a decision really needs.
Show totals and counts in reports; keep names and phone numbers only in operational lists for staff who must act on them.
Give access by role: a branch manager sees her branch, not every customer in the company.
Do not share raw exports in WhatsApp groups or personal email. Share a link with access control, or a summary without personal details.
Use strong, unique passwords and two-step verification on every BI and source account, and remove access the day someone leaves.
Keep health, salary and similar sensitive data out of general dashboards entirely.

blocks.title: Scam and leak warning
blocks.text: Customer lists with phone numbers and balances are valuable to fraudsters. Never send them to someone who claims, by phone or chat, to be from a bank, regulator or "IT support". Confirm through a known official contact first.

takeaways: Measure completeness, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness, validity and accuracy
Fix data problems at the source, then monitor them every refresh
Every metric has one owner, and every definition change is logged
Mark certified reports so leaders know which numbers to quote
Load only the personal data you need, restrict access by role, and never share raw exports casually

activity.title: Write a one-page governance plan
steps: Choose one dataset from your source map
Write one check for at least four of the six quality dimensions
Run the checks if you have the data, or estimate, and record the scores
Name an owner for each of your top five metrics and a data steward
List three data protection rules the organisation will follow
activity.evidence: A one-page governance plan with quality checks, scores, owners and protection rules

quiz.q: A data source map rates the attendance register: access 1, quality 2, frequency 1. The fee export scores 8 out of 9. What should the designer do?
options: Build the attendance report first because attendance matters most
Use fees in the first release and plan a digital register before using attendance
Drop attendance from the design permanently
Average the two sources into one score
quiz.explain: A total of 4 shows attendance is not ready. Fees are ready now; attendance needs data work first.

quiz.q: A school bills ₦30,000,000 in fees for a term and receives ₦24,600,000. What is the fee collection rate?
A decision scores value 5 and feasibility 1. Where does it sit and what should happen?
options: Quick win: build it this week
Major project: start data collection work before building reports
Fill-in: build when convenient
It should be deleted from the inventory
quiz.explain: High value but low feasibility is a major project; the data must be prepared first.

quiz.q: Which report best suits a depot supervisor each morning?
options: A 12-month revenue trend chart
A list of retailers more than 30 days overdue to call today
A quarterly board pack
A pie chart of product share
quiz.explain: Operational reports should be action lists that tell staff exactly what to do today.

quiz.q: A register has 2,000 records and 160 are missing a phone number. What is the completeness score for phone numbers?
A manager wants to change the definition of "active customer" from 3 months to 6 months. What should happen under good governance?
options: She edits the report formula herself
The metric owner approves it and the change is recorded in the change log
Each report keeps its own version
The BI analyst decides quietly
quiz.explain: Only the metric owner approves changes, and every change is logged so past figures stay explainable.

quiz.q: A branch manager asks for the full customer list with phone numbers and balances to be posted in the staff WhatsApp group. What is the best response?
options: Post it, since staff work for the company
Share a role-based link or a summary, and keep personal details only with staff who must act on them
Email it to everyone instead
Print it and leave copies at reception
quiz.explain: Personal data should be shared only on a need-to-know basis with access control, in line with data protection practice.

modules.title: Leading BI Work: Discovery, Pricing, Adoption and Portfolio
modules.overview: You learn to run discovery with decision-makers, price and scope a BI strategy engagement, and lead the adoption that makes the system worth its cost. You finish with a roadmap and a portfolio case study.

lessons.title: Discovery with decision-makers: interviews, stakeholder lists and the current-state report
objectives: Plan a one-week BI discovery with the right people in the right order
Ask interview questions that uncover decisions, not just data wishes
Turn interview notes into decision inventory entries
Write and present a short current-state report

blocks.text: Discovery is where BI projects are won or lost. If you only talk to the IT officer about systems, you will design reports about data. If you talk to the people who make decisions, you will design reports that change what they do. Good discovery is short, structured and focused on **decisions, pain and evidence**.

blocks.name: interview
blocks.alt: Two people in a structured interview conversation
blocks.caption: Discovery interviews focus on the decisions people make and what slows them down.

blocks.text: Who to talk to

items: **The sponsor**: the person paying for the work or championing it, often the owner, CEO or executive director. Agree the goal and budget with them first.
**Decision-makers**: the people in the decision inventory, from the owner to branch managers.
**Data keepers**: whoever enters, exports or controls the data in each source system.
**Report makers**: whoever builds the current reports by hand. They know where every problem hides.
**Report readers outside**: if donors, regulators or a board receive reports, find out exactly what they require.

blocks.title: A one-week discovery
items: Day 1: sponsor kick-off
Days 2 to 3: interviews
Day 4: source review
Day 5: findings playback
blocks.caption: A short, fixed timetable keeps discovery focused and shows the client progress quickly.

blocks.text: Questions that reveal decisions
Avoid asking "What reports do you want?" People will list every chart they have ever seen. Ask about their work instead.

head: Area
Questions
rows: What decisions do you make every week or month? Which one costs the most when it goes wrong?
What do you look at before you decide? Where does it come from? How old is it by the time you see it?
Tell me about the last time the numbers were wrong or late. What happened?
Who prepares the report you use? How many hours does it take each time?
Which systems hold this information? Who can export it? Is any of it on paper?
If this worked perfectly in six months, what would you be doing differently?

blocks.text: Listen for numbers and stories. "The quarterly donor report takes my team two days per state" is far more useful than "reporting is stressful". Write down exact phrases; they will go into your report and help the sponsor recognise their own organisation.

blocks.title: Worked example: discovery for an NGO skills programme
blocks.context: Amina (for example) runs discovery for an NGO that trains young women in tailoring and digital skills in 4 states and reports quarterly to two donors.
steps: The programme director says her biggest decision is where to move trainers and funds each quarter. Today she decides from memory and phone calls, because the donor report arrives a month after the quarter ends.

Each of the 4 state coordinators spends about 2 days per quarter compiling attendance and completion figures from paper and Google Forms. That is 4 x 2 = 8 person-days per quarter, or 8 x 4 = 32 person-days a year.
The two donors define "completion" differently: one counts 80% attendance, the other requires passing a final assessment. Coordinators keep two separate tallies.

Amina writes three decision inventory entries: quarterly reallocation of trainers and funds (director), monthly follow-up of at-risk trainees (state coordinators), quarterly donor reporting (M&E officer).
She adds a metric dictionary note: two completion definitions are needed, each owned by the M&E officer and labelled by donor.
blocks.result: The discovery shows that a monthly state-by-state view of enrolment, attendance and both completion measures would serve the director's decision and cut most of the 32 person-days a year of manual compiling.

blocks.text: Many interviews will happen by phone, WhatsApp call or Zoom, especially across states. Ask permission before recording, keep each call to 30 to 45 minutes, and type up your notes the same day while details are fresh. Send each person a three-line summary of what you heard so they can correct anything you misunderstood.
The current-state report
End discovery with a short report, five to eight pages at most, and present it in a playback meeting. Structure:

items: **Goal**: the sponsor's goal in one or two sentences, in their words.
**Decisions**: the decision inventory, ranked by value and feasibility.
**Current state**: maturity score, the source map with ratings, and the main pain points with real examples and hours spent.
**Key issues**: conflicting definitions, quality problems, access or privacy risks.
**Recommendation**: the first release (two or three decisions), what data work is needed first, and the proposed next phase.
**Questions still open** and who will answer them.

blocks.title: Confirm before you build
blocks.text: In the playback meeting, ask the sponsor to confirm the top three decisions in writing, for example by replying to your summary email. This agreement protects you later when new requests appear.

blocks.title: Handle access carefully
blocks.text: During discovery, ask to see sample exports or screens, not passwords. If you must log into a system, ask the owner to create a separate account for you with read-only access, and ask for it to be removed when the project ends.

takeaways: Talk first to the sponsor, then decision-makers, data keepers and report makers
Ask about decisions, pain, effort and success, not about wished-for charts
Capture real numbers such as hours spent and days of delay
End with a short current-state report and get written agreement on priorities
Request read-only accounts, never other people's passwords

activity.title: Run one discovery interview
steps: Choose one decision-maker in an organisation you know
Ask at least six questions from the table, one from each area
Write down exact phrases and any numbers they mention
Turn the answers into two decision inventory entries
Write a half-page current-state summary for that person's area
activity.evidence: Interview notes, two inventory entries and a half-page summary

lessons.title: Pricing a BI strategy engagement and controlling scope
objectives: Choose between fixed-fee, phased and retainer pricing for BI work
Estimate an engagement from task-level days and add contingency
Write the scope, assumptions and exclusions sections of a proposal
Handle new requests with a simple change request process

blocks.text: BI strategy work is senior work. You are helping leaders decide how information will flow through their organisation for years. Price it on the effort and expertise involved, write down exactly what is included, and protect both sides with a clear agreement.

blocks.name: contract
blocks.alt: A signed contract document with a pen
blocks.caption: A written scope and payment schedule protect both you and the client.

blocks.text: Three common pricing models

head: Model
What it covers
Good when
Risk
rows: Discovery, source map, metric dictionary, reporting design, roadmap
Scope is clear after a short first conversation
Scope creep if exclusions are not written
Separate fee per phase: foundations, first release, next release
Client may stop after phase one
A fixed number of days each month for governance, quality checks, new reports, training
After launch, to keep the system healthy
Unused days cause disputes unless rules are clear

blocks.text: Estimating from tasks

Do not guess a single total. List the tasks, estimate the days for each, multiply by your day rate, then add contingency for the unknowns. Your day rate depends on your experience, the client's size and your market. The rate below is only an example to show the method, not a market price.

blocks.title: Worked example: a strategy engagement for a pharmacy chain
blocks.context: Kemi (for example) is quoting a BI strategy and roadmap for a pharmacy chain with five branches in Lagos. She uses an example day rate of ₦75,000.
steps: Discovery interviews and site visits: 4 days. Source assessment and data source map: 3 days. Metric dictionary for 15 metrics: 3 days. Reporting structure and wireframes: 2 days. Roadmap, governance plan and final presentation: 2 days.
Total effort: 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 14 days.
Contingency of 15% for unknown data problems: ₦1,050,000 x 0.15 = ₦157,500.
Payment schedule 40% / 40% / 20%: ₦483,000 at signing, ₦483,000 after the current-state report, ₦241,500 after the final presentation.
blocks.result: Kemi's proposal shows the task list and days, so the client sees what they are paying for. A follow-on retainer of 2 days a month would be 2 x ₦75,000 = ₦150,000 a month at the same example rate.

blocks.text: Scope: in and out

blocks.title: Writing the scope
items: In scope
Out of scope
blocks.caption: Listing what is excluded is as important as listing what is included; it is where most disputes start.

blocks.text: A proposal should also list **assumptions**: what the client must provide and by when. For example: "The client will provide exports from the POS and accounting system within 5 working days of signing" and "Interviews will be scheduled within the first two weeks." If an assumption fails, the timeline or fee can be reviewed.
What the proposal contains

items: **Background**: the client's goal in their words, from discovery.
**Deliverables**: each document or report, described so that both sides can tell when it is finished.
**Approach and timeline**: the phases, the meetings and the dates.
**Scope, exclusions and assumptions**, as above.
**Fee and payment schedule**, with what triggers each payment.
**Confidentiality and data handling**: how you will store, use and delete the client's data at the end.

blocks.text: For retainers, write how unused days are treated (for example, they do not roll over, or they roll over for one month only), how requests are submitted, and how quickly you respond. Send a short monthly note listing the days used and the work done, so the client sees the value of the retainer every month.
Handling new requests

items: Thank the person and write the request down exactly.
Check it against the written scope. If it is already included, schedule it.
If it is new, estimate the extra days and the effect on the deadline.
Send a short change request: what, why, days, cost, new date.
Start only after the sponsor approves it in writing, even by email or a WhatsApp message you keep.

blocks.title: Protect the money
blocks.text: Issue a proper invoice with your business name and bank details, and receive payment by traceable bank transfer. Confirm that money has actually arrived in your own bank app before releasing work. Payment screenshots and "debit alerts" forwarded by someone else can be faked. If you operate as a business, register it with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) so your invoices and contracts carry a registered name.

blocks.title: Price the value, explain the effort
blocks.text: When a client says the fee is high, go back to the discovery numbers. If the organisation spends 32 person-days a year compiling one report, or loses money on late reorders every month, show how the design addresses that. Do not cut days without cutting scope.

takeaways: Use fixed fee for clear strategy work, phases for big projects, retainers after launch
Estimate task by task, multiply by your rate, add contingency
Write scope, exclusions and client assumptions in the proposal
New requests go through a written change request before work starts
Invoice properly and confirm payment in your own bank app

activity.title: Draft a priced proposal outline
steps: Take the organisation from your discovery interview
List five to seven tasks and estimate days for each
Choose your own day rate and calculate base fee, contingency and total
Write four in-scope and four out-of-scope items
Write a payment schedule and two client assumptions
activity.evidence: A one-page proposal outline with task days, fee calculation, scope and payment schedule

lessons.title: Leading adoption, measuring impact and building your BI portfolio
objectives: Plan training and routines that get BI reports used in real decisions
Measure adoption and impact with simple, honest metrics
Write a now, next, later BI roadmap
Assemble a BI strategy case study for your portfolio

blocks.text: A BI system is only finished when people use it to decide. Many technically good projects fail quietly: the dashboard launches, usage fades within weeks, and managers return to their private spreadsheets. As the BI lead, adoption is your job, not an afterthought.

blocks.name: team-collaboration
blocks.alt: A team working together around shared screens
blocks.caption: Adoption happens in meetings and routines, not at the launch event.

blocks.text: What drives adoption

items: **Use it in the meeting.** The sponsor opens the report at the start of the weekly or monthly meeting and asks questions from it. When the leader uses it, others follow.
**Retire the old reports.** If the old manual report still arrives, people will keep using it. Agree a date to stop it.
**Train by role, briefly.** A 30-minute session per role, using their own data and their own decisions, works better than a long general training.
**Choose champions.** One person in each branch or department who is comfortable with the report and helps colleagues.
**Make feedback easy.** A simple form or WhatsApp number for "this number looks wrong" reports, with a promise to reply within two working days.

blocks.text: Measuring adoption and impact
Track a few honest measures for the first three months after launch:

head: Measure
How to calculate
Why it matters
rows: Intended users who opened the report in the period, divided by all intended users
Shows whether people look at it
Number of decisions recorded in meeting notes that used the report
Shows whether it changes what people do
Hours spent compiling reports before, minus hours after
Problems reported and the share fixed within the promised time
Shows whether trust is being protected

blocks.title: Worked example: an eight-week adoption review
blocks.context: Chidi (for example) reviews the beverage distributor's BI system eight weeks after launch. Twenty managers and supervisors were meant to use the reports.
steps: Active users: 14 of 20 opened the weekly report at least once a week. Rate: 14 / 20 x 100 = 70%.
He checks who is missing: all 6 non-users work at the depot with the weakest mobile network. He arranges a PDF summary on WhatsApp for them each Monday.

Time saved: before, 2 staff spent 3 days each per month compiling reports, 2 x 3 = 6 person-days. Now 1 person spends 1 day checking the refresh. Saving: 6 - 1 = 5 person-days a month, or 5 x 12 = 60 person-days a year.
Decisions logged: the meeting notes show 9 reorder decisions and 3 credit limit changes made using the reports.
Quality: 7 issues reported, 6 fixed within two working days. Rate: 6 / 7 x 100 = about 86%.
blocks.result: Chidi reports to the owner with numbers, not impressions, and his next action is aimed at the real cause of low use: network access at one depot.

blocks.text: The BI roadmap: now, next, later

blocks.title: A three-horizon BI roadmap
items: Now: top 3 decisions
Next: fix weak sources
Later: forecasting and alerts
blocks.caption: A roadmap in three horizons shows leaders the path without promising exact dates for uncertain work.

blocks.text: **Now** (the current quarter) covers the first release and governance basics. **Next** covers the sources and decisions that needed data work, such as digitising attendance or recording retailer locations. **Later** covers advanced work such as forecasting, which only makes sense once history is clean. Review the roadmap with the sponsor every quarter.
Your BI portfolio

Tool skills are shown by dashboards. BI strategy skills are shown by **the documents that come before the dashboard**. Build one strong case study, for a real organisation with permission, or for a realistic invented one clearly labelled as a practice case.

items: **Context**: the organisation type, size and goal, without confidential details.
**Decision inventory**: ranked by value and feasibility.
**Maturity score and data source map** with ratings.
**Metric dictionary**: at least five complete entries.
**Reporting structure**: three tiers and the rhythm of business.
**Governance plan**: quality checks, owners, data protection rules.
**Results or expected impact**: adoption and time-saved numbers if real, clearly marked estimates if not.

blocks.title: Protect client data in your portfolio
blocks.text: Remove names, phone numbers, account details and real financial figures unless the client agrees in writing. Replace them with realistic sample values and say so. A portfolio that leaks client data will cost you more work than it wins.

Paths after this course differ by where you want to work. Inside an organisation, the natural step is from analyst or report builder to BI lead, owning priorities and governance. As a consultant, the strategy pack from your capstone becomes your first offer to clients. Either way, keep building tool depth alongside strategy, so you can judge what your designs will cost to build.

When you present your case study to a future client or employer, lead with the decision you improved and the time or money it affected, then show the documents. This is what separates a BI lead from someone who only builds charts.

takeaways: Adoption comes from leaders using reports in meetings and old reports being retired
Measure active users, decisions logged, time saved and quality issue fixes
Investigate low usage for its real cause before blaming users
Present the roadmap in now, next and later horizons
A BI portfolio shows the design documents and the decisions they improved

activity.title: Plan adoption and start your case study
steps: Write the adoption plan for your design: meetings, training, champions, old reports to retire
Choose three adoption measures and how you will calculate them
Draft a now, next, later roadmap with two items in each horizon
Create the context and decision inventory sections of your portfolio case study
activity.evidence: An adoption plan, a three-horizon roadmap and the first two sections of your case study

quiz.q: In a discovery interview, which question is most likely to reveal a real decision need?
options: Which charts do you like?
Tell me about the last time the numbers were late or wrong. What happened?
Do you prefer bar charts or pie charts?
How many reports do you want?
quiz.explain: Asking about a real incident uncovers the decision, its cost and the information gap.

quiz.q: Three state coordinators each spend 3 days per quarter compiling a donor report. How many person-days is that per year?
quiz.explain: 3 coordinators x 3 days = 9 person-days per quarter; 9 x 4 quarters = 36 per year.

quiz.q: An engagement is estimated at 12 days at an example rate of ₦80,000 a day, with 10% contingency. What is the quoted fee?
Midway through a project the client asks you to also build the dashboards in Power BI, which your proposal listed as out of scope. What should you do?
options: Build them quietly to keep the client happy
Refuse and end the project
Estimate the extra days and cost, send a change request, and start after written approval
Remove another deliverable without telling them
quiz.explain: New work goes through a written change request so the fee and deadline are agreed first.

quiz.q: Eight weeks after launch, 12 of 30 intended users open the report weekly, and most non-users are in branches with poor network. What is the best next step?
options: Report a 60% active user rate and move on
Add a light summary delivered by WhatsApp or PDF for those branches and keep measuring
Retrain everyone for a full day
Remove those branches from the system
quiz.explain: 12 / 30 = 40% active. The cause is access, so fix delivery for those users.

quiz.q: A client says your BI strategy portfolio piece only shows a dashboard screenshot. What would best demonstrate strategy skills?
options: More colourful dashboards
The decision inventory, source map, metric dictionary, reporting structure and governance plan behind it
A list of tools you have used
A longer CV
quiz.explain: Strategy skill is shown by the design documents and the decisions they improved.

finalQuiz.q: Which statement best describes a business intelligence system?
options: A dashboard tool such as Power BI
A repeating system that gets the right information to the right decision-maker at the right time
A large store of raw data files
A one-off report for the board
finalQuiz.explain: Tools are parts; BI is the whole chain from sources to decisions and action.

finalQuiz.q: A table's grain is "one row per receipt line". The owner wants daily totals per branch. What is true?
options: The table cannot give daily totals
Daily totals can be added up from receipt lines
A second table with a different grain must be mixed into it
The grain must be changed to daily
finalQuiz.explain: Detailed rows can always be summed up to daily totals, but not the other way round.

finalQuiz.q: "At the current rate of sales, cooking oil will run out in 6 days." What kind of analysis is this?
options: Descriptive
Diagnostic
Predictive
Prescriptive
finalQuiz.explain: It estimates what is likely to happen, which is predictive.

finalQuiz.q: An organisation scores 15 out of 20 on the maturity check. Which level and next step fit best?
options: Level 2: merge spreadsheets
Level 3: create a trusted store
Level 4: link each report to a decision meeting and track actions
Level 5: start forecasting immediately
finalQuiz.explain: 14 to 17 is level 4 (managed). The next step is tying reports to decisions and tracking actions.

finalQuiz.q: A source is rated access 2, quality 1, frequency 3. What is its total and what does the low score suggest?
options: 6; quality work is needed before relying on it
5; it is ready now
6; it should be deleted
9; it is the best source
finalQuiz.explain: 2 + 1 + 3 = 6. A quality score of 1 means the data needs cleaning or better entry rules first.

finalQuiz.q: Which item makes a metric dictionary entry complete?
options: A nice chart of the metric
Formula, inclusions and exclusions, source, owner and refresh
Only the metric name
The name of the BI tool
finalQuiz.explain: Without exclusions, an owner and a refresh time, people will calculate the metric differently.

finalQuiz.q: Decision A scores value 4 x feasibility 5. Decision B scores value 5 x feasibility 2. Which should be built first and why?
options: B, because value matters more than anything
A, because its priority score is 20 against B's 10
Both at once in one dashboard
Neither, until all data is perfect
finalQuiz.explain: 4 x 5 = 20 and 5 x 2 = 10, so A is a quick win. B needs data work first.

finalQuiz.q: Which report belongs in the strategic tier?
options: Today's delivery list for drivers
A list of overdue retailers to call
A monthly one-page view of 6 headline metrics against targets with 12-month trends
A real-time stock alert
finalQuiz.explain: Strategic reports serve owners and boards with few metrics, trends and targets, monthly or quarterly.

finalQuiz.q: A register has 800 records; 24 are duplicates of IDs already listed. What is the uniqueness score?
Which practice best follows data protection principles when designing BI reports?
options: Put every customer's phone number on the main dashboard
Show totals in reports and restrict personal details to staff who must act on them
Email raw exports to all managers weekly
Keep one shared password for the BI account
finalQuiz.explain: Load only needed personal data, show aggregates, and control access by role.

finalQuiz.q: Your estimate is 10 days at an example rate of ₦70,000 plus 20% contingency. What do you quote?
Which evidence best shows a BI system is having impact after launch?
options: The number of charts on the dashboard
Decisions logged in meetings using the reports, active user rate and time saved
The cost of the BI tool
The launch event attendance
finalQuiz.explain: Impact is measured by use in decisions and real time saved, not by the size of the dashboard.

capstone.title: BI Strategy and System Design Project
capstone.brief: Produce a complete BI strategy pack for one real or realistic organisation: a decision inventory, a data source map and reporting structure for the top decisions, and a governance plan for metric definitions, data quality and long-term maintenance.
steps: Choose an organisation and agree access with its leader, or build a clearly labelled practice case
Run at least three discovery interviews and a 10-question maturity check
Write a decision inventory of at least eight decisions, scored for value and feasibility
Build a data source map with access, quality and frequency ratings for every source
Write metric dictionary entries for at least five key metrics
Design the three-tier reporting structure and the rhythm of business for the top three decisions
Write a governance plan: six quality checks, metric owners, change log, data protection rules and a now, next, later roadmap
Present the pack in a short playback to the leader or a peer and note their feedback
evidence: Decision inventory with value x feasibility scores
Reporting structure with tiers and cadence
